findings.title: Python's hash() on str is randomized per process
findings.body: `hash(group_key) % num_queues` uses Python's salted string hash. Two consumers, or a consumer after restart, map the same subscription to different queues. Per-subscription ordering therefore holds only inside one process. After a rebalance or restart, in-flight work on the old process and new work on the new one can run out of order. A stable hash such as crc32 or md5 should be used.

findings.title: Partition revocation/rebalance not handled; no backpressure
findings.body: Queues are unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit` never blocks or raises MessageRejected. The docstring claims 'Natural backpressure', but a slow worker lets queued items grow without limit in memory. Separately, the shared pool and OffsetTracker outlive the strategy. `create_with_partitions` creates a new strategy on every rebalance, and `close()` shuts down the pool owned by the factory. A second strategy then reuses a shut-down pool with dead workers and stale offsets from revoked partitions.

findings.title: queue.ShutDown requires Python 3.13
findings.body: `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` exist only in Python 3.13+. On older interpreters, evaluating `except queue.ShutDown` raises AttributeError only when an exception actually occurs. `q.shutdown` is also missing, so the workers never wake from the blocking `get()` and the join times out. Sentry's supported Python version should be checked, or a sentinel used instead.

findings.title: Shutdown can drop or hang on queued items; worker break skips remaining work
findings.body: In `run`, `except queue.ShutDown: break` inside the processing block exits without being a normal path. The `finally` still completes the offset, so an item can be marked complete even though it was not processed. The `shutdown` flag is also checked only between items. The commit thread is joined before the pool is drained, so items finished during shutdown never get committed.

findings.title: Unsynchronized shared dict mutation and O(range) commit scan
findings.body: `all_offsets`, `outstanding` and `last_committed` are defaultdicts. They get mutated, with new keys created, under different per-partition locks. The lock creation itself (`get` then `setdefault`) is fine. `get_committable_offsets` iterates over every integer from start to max_offset. After large gaps, for example compacted topics or offsets skipped by filtering, this becomes very slow while holding the lock that workers need.

findings.title: Errors in result processing still commit offsets (data loss)
findings.body: The worker's `finally` always calls `complete_offset`, even when processing raised. Failed messages are therefore committed and lost. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts that no commit happens, which contradicts this behavior. It passes only because the commit loop runs once per second and the test checks sooner.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the wrong thing and is timing-dependent
findings.body: The test claims errors do not block commits for other messages but asserts that nothing is committed. This passes only because the commit loop has not yet run (1s interval) within the roughly 0.3s window. It will be flaky, and it does not verify the intended behavior.
